title: Reducing restrictive practice
blurb: Recognise every form of restrictive practice, apply the tests of lawful, necessary and proportionate use, and work to reduce it.
question: In a supported living service, staff lock the kitchen at night because Ruth, 38, who has Prader-Willi syndrome, takes food. A new nurse is asked whether this is acceptable. How should she assess it?

teach.body: NICE NG11 defines restrictive interventions as interventions that may infringe a person's human rights and freedom of movement, including locking doors, preventing access to parts of the living space, seclusion, manual and mechanical restraint, rapid tranquillisation and long-term sedation. In plain English: anything that stops a person doing what they want, or moving where they want, is restrictive, even when it is meant kindly.

teach.caption: Mechanical and environmental restrictions, and 'as required' medicine for behaviour, are easy to overlook.

teach.body: NICE NG11: reactive strategies are a last resort and used together with proactive support, although when risks are significant or a placement is close to breaking down they may be the initial intervention, with proactive support introduced once things stabilise (1.9.1). Planned restrictive interventions must be within the legal framework (Human Rights Act, Mental Health Act, Mental Capacity Act and DoLS), in the person's best interests to protect them or others from immediate and significant harm, and a reasonable, necessary and proportionate response to the risk. Use a graded approach, least restrictive first, and pair every restriction with a reduction programme.

root.label: Is there a lawful basis?
root.sub: Consent, MCA best interests, MHA, DoLS

children.label: Is it necessary to prevent harm?

teach.h: Restraint under the Mental Capacity Act
teach.body: Under MCA s6, restraint means using or threatening force to make someone do something they resist, or restricting their movement whether or not they resist. For a person who lacks capacity it is lawful only if the person acting reasonably believes it is necessary to prevent harm to the person, and it is a proportionate response to the likelihood and seriousness of that harm. Restraint that amounts to a deprivation of liberty needs separate authorisation.

head: Source
Key point
rows: No restraint affecting airway, breathing, circulation
No deliberate face-down restraint on any surface
De-escalate first; one person leads the hold throughout
teach.caption: Seni's Law applies to mental health units, including learning disability and autism inpatient units; ss1-5 and most of s6 in force 31 March 2022 (s6(5)(n), recording death or serious injury, is not yet in force).
NICE NG11 1.9.3-1.9.6: document, discuss with everyone involved, and use it to improve the plan.

teach.h: Scenario: Ruth and the locked kitchen
teach.body: Ruth, 38, has Prader-Willi syndrome and extreme hunger, so food security protects her health. But a locked kitchen is an environmental restriction. The nurse checks: has Ruth's capacity to decide about food access been assessed; if she lacks it, is there a recorded best interests decision; is this the least restrictive option (a locked food cupboard rather than the whole kitchen, planned snack times); is it recorded, reviewed, and could it amount to a deprivation of liberty that needs authorisation?

teach.text: Do not confuse 'for her own good' with 'lawful'. A restriction needs a lawful basis, necessity, proportionality and the least restrictive option. Also, a restriction used on everyone in a service (blanket rule) because of one person's risk is rarely justified.

items: Restrictive practice includes physical, mechanical, chemical, environmental, seclusion and blanket rules.
Last resort, lawful, best interests, necessary and proportionate, least restrictive first (NG11 1.9).
MCA s6: restraint only to prevent harm and proportionate to its likelihood and seriousness.
Never restrain in a way that affects airway, breathing or circulation; no deliberate face-down restraint.
Record, debrief, review and pair every restriction with a reduction programme.

summary: You can now recognise all forms of restrictive practice, test any restriction for lawfulness, necessity, proportionality and least restriction, and follow the safety rules for restraint. You can record, debrief and work towards reducing restrictive practice.

A.q: Which of the following is a restrictive practice according to the NICE NG11 definition?
options: Offering a person a choice of two activities
Locking a door to stop a person entering a room
Using a visual timetable for the day ahead
A person choosing to spend time in their own room
A.why: NG11 lists locking doors and preventing a person entering areas of their living space as restrictive interventions.

whyNot.2: A visual timetable is a proactive support.
whyNot.3: Time alone by choice is not restrictive.

A.q: NICE NG11 says planned restrictive interventions must be which of the following?
options: Agreed by a family member before use
Recorded weekly in the care plan
Reasonable, necessary and proportionate
Approved by the local authority first
A.why: NG11 1.9.5: within the legal framework, in the person's best interests to protect from immediate and significant harm, and a reasonable, necessary and proportionate response to the risk.

whyNot.0: Families should be involved in planning, but agreement is not the legal test.
whyNot.1: Every use is documented; weekly recording is not the test.
whyNot.3: Local authority authorisation applies to DoLS, not every restrictive intervention.

A.q: Positive and Proactive Care (2014) says staff must not deliberately restrain people in which way?
options: In a seated position on a chair
On their side on a bed
Using a two-person escort hold
Face down on any surface
A.why: The guidance says staff must not deliberately restrain in a way that affects airway, breathing or circulation, such as face-down restraint on any surface.

whyNot.0: Seated holds are not the position named in the guidance.
whyNot.1: Side-lying is not the position the guidance prohibits.
whyNot.2: Escort holds are not the prohibited position.

B.q: Dan, 32, has a severe learning disability and lacks capacity about personal care. He resists having his teeth brushed and staff propose holding his hands. Under MCA s6, when would this be lawful?
options: When it is necessary to prevent harm and proportionate
When his family has agreed to the hold in writing
When two trained members of staff carry out the hold
When it is recorded in his care plan as a routine
B.why: MCA s6: restraint is lawful only if reasonably believed necessary to prevent harm to the person and proportionate to the likelihood and seriousness of that harm. Less restrictive approaches should be tried first.

whyNot.1: Family agreement does not make restraint lawful under s6.
whyNot.2: Training and staff numbers do not meet the legal test.
whyNot.3: Making restraint routine does not establish necessity or proportionality.

B.q: In a residential service, every resident's bedroom is locked during the day because one resident took others' belongings. What is the main concern?
options: The locks should be on the communal rooms instead
Each resident should consent to the lock in writing
The locks need a fire safety risk assessment first
It is a blanket restriction affecting everyone
B.why: A restriction applied to everyone because of one person's risk is a blanket restriction; it restricts people who pose no risk and is rarely proportionate.

whyNot.0: Moving locks to other rooms is still a blanket restriction.
whyNot.1: Written consent does not address the blanket nature.
whyNot.2: Fire safety matters, but the main issue is the unjustified restriction.

B.q: Mark, 41, has a learning disability and is restrained by staff during an incident in a learning disability inpatient unit. Under the Mental Health Units (Use of Force) Act 2018, what must happen?
options: A doctor must review him within 15 minutes
The use of force must be recorded
His nearest relative must be informed
The CQC must be told the same day
B.why: Section 6 of the Use of Force Act requires the unit to record each use of force (negligible force excepted), including the reason and the type of force.

whyNot.0: This timeframe is not a requirement of the Act.
whyNot.2: Informing relatives may be good practice but is not the s6 duty.
whyNot.3: The Act does not require same-day notification to the CQC for each use.

C.q: Ruth, 38, has Prader-Willi syndrome. Staff lock the whole kitchen at night to stop her taking food. She has not had a capacity assessment about food access. What should the nurse do first?
options: Leave the lock as it protects Ruth from serious harm
Assess Ruth's capacity to decide about access to food
Remove the lock at once and rely on staff checks
Ask Ruth's mother to agree to the lock as next of kin
C.why: Any restriction needs a lawful basis. The first step is to assess Ruth's capacity about this decision; if she lacks it, a best interests decision must consider the least restrictive option.

whyNot.0: A risk to health does not by itself make the restriction lawful or least restrictive.
whyNot.2: Removing food security suddenly may cause harm; a lawful, planned review is needed.
whyNot.3: Being next of kin gives her mother no power to consent for an adult; if Ruth lacks capacity, a best interests decision is the process.

C.q: After Ali, 25, who is autistic, is held by staff during an incident, he is calm and uninjured. What should happen next, in line with NICE NG11?
options: Close the incident as he is unharmed
Increase his PRN medication to prevent recurrence
Restrict his community access for one week
Record, debrief and review his support plan
C.why: NG11 1.9.3-1.9.6: document and review the intervention, discuss with everyone involved including Ali and his family, and use it to inform his behaviour support plan.

whyNot.0: Lack of injury does not remove the need to record, debrief and learn.
whyNot.1: Increasing medication is a restrictive response and not the learning step.
whyNot.2: Restricting access is punitive and adds restriction.

C.q: A plan for Gemma, 30, includes a two-person hold when she bites others. The hold has been used daily for a month with no fall in incidents. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Review the functional assessment and proactive strategies
Add a longer hold time to the existing reactive plan
Train more staff so the hold is applied more quickly
Request rapid tranquillisation as the next step
C.why: Frequent restraint without improvement means the plan is not meeting Gemma's needs. NG11 requires every restrictive intervention to be accompanied by a reduction programme within the behaviour support plan.

whyNot.1: Longer holds increase risk and restriction.
whyNot.2: Faster restraint does not address why she bites.
whyNot.3: Escalating to rapid tranquillisation adds restriction without understanding the cause.

reteach.title: Four questions before any restriction
reteach.question: Before you stop someone doing something, what must you be able to answer?

blocks.body: Ask: What gives me the legal right (consent, MCA best interests, MHA, DoLS)? Is it needed to prevent real harm? Is the response in proportion to that harm? Is there anything less restrictive that would work? If you cannot answer all four, do not restrict, and escalate.

blocks.text: Locked doors, removed belongings and 'as required' sedation are restrictive too, not just holds.

explain.body: Physical, mechanical, chemical, environmental, seclusion and blanket rules. NG11 includes locking doors, rapid tranquillisation and long-term sedation.

test.q: Which is an example of chemical restraint?
options: A sedative given to manage behaviour
An antibiotic given for a chest infection
Paracetamol for dental pain
A laxative for constipation
test.why: Medicine used to control behaviour or restrict movement, rather than to treat a diagnosed condition, is chemical restraint.

explain.body: NG11 1.9.5: lawful framework, best interests to protect from immediate and significant harm, reasonable, necessary and proportionate.

test.q: Which phrase best describes when NICE NG11 allows a planned restrictive intervention?
options: When staff on shift feel unsafe
When the person refuses planned care
When harm is immediate and significant
When the family requests it in writing
test.why: NG11 1.9.5 refers to protecting the person or others from immediate and significant harm.

whyNot.0: Staff feelings alone do not meet the test.
whyNot.1: Refusal of care is not itself harm.
whyNot.3: A family request does not establish necessity.

explain.body: No restraint that affects airway, breathing or circulation; no deliberate face-down restraint (Positive and Proactive Care, 2014). One staff member leads throughout and makes sure others can protect the head and neck, check airway and breathing and monitor vital signs (NICE NG10 1.4.32).
explain.cite: DH Positive and Proactive Care 2014; NICE NG10 1.4.32

test.q: According to NICE NG10, how should a manual restraint be led?
options: The nurse in charge takes over the lead on arrival
One person leads throughout and ensures airway checks
Staff rotate the lead role every few minutes
A doctor leads the hold once called to the scene
test.why: NG10 1.4.32: one staff member should lead throughout the use of manual restraint and make sure other staff can protect the head and neck, check that airway and breathing are not compromised and monitor vital signs.

whyNot.0: NG10 says one staff member leads throughout; handing over to whoever arrives breaks that continuity.
whyNot.2: Rotating the lead conflicts with one person leading throughout the restraint.
whyNot.3: The lead is a member of the team carrying out the hold; safety checks cannot wait for a doctor.

explain.body: Mental Health Units (Use of Force) Act 2018: responsible person, policy, information, training, recording. Applies to LD and autism inpatient units.

test.q: Which setting does the Mental Health Units (Use of Force) Act 2018 apply to?
options: Supported living services
Residential care homes
Mental health inpatient units
Special schools for children
test.why: The Act applies to mental health units in England, including learning disability and autism inpatient units.

whyNot.0: Supported living is not a mental health unit.
whyNot.1: Care homes are outside the Act.
